source: Elexon Insights, Market Index Data (APX), half-hourly GB prices
method: upper bound: perfect foresight, one full cycle per day; per day (mean of the top d hours' price - mean of the bottom d hours' price) x d MWh per MW x round-trip efficiency 0.85, summed over the days; charge and discharge hours are not forced into order
derivation: 17520 APX rows from https://data.elexon.co.uk/bmrs/api/v1/datasets/MID/stream?from=2025-09-27&to=2026-09-26&settlementPeriodFrom=1&settlementPeriodTo=50&dataProviders=APXMIDP; 364 days with >= 44 priced half hours kept; 2h: GBP 44,705/MW/yr, 4h: GBP 79,704/MW/yr, 8h: GBP 120,972/MW/yr
note: Snapshot of the live computation on 2026-09-27 (bessible.market.refresh). Served only when the live source fails, and then flagged cached.
cross_check: Modo Energy, "How does a battery energy storage system make money?", Neil Weaver, 19 May 2026 (updated 21 May 2026), https://modoenergy.com/research/en/how-does-battery-energy-storage-make-money: "In GB, wholesale and Balancing Mechanism revenues together averaged £43,829/MW/year over the twelve months to April 2026." Not the same measure as ours: it includes Balancing Mechanism revenue, covers realised (not perfect-foresight) trading, a different period, and states no duration. The same page gives "A typical two-hour GB BESS earned £73,145/MW/year over the twelve months to April 2026."; the page also says "Two-hour GB BESS revenue averaged £73,145/MW/year over the twelve months to April 2026, with wholesale and Balancing Mechanism revenues making up around 60% of the stack" (in the page HTML twice, in a summary block). £43,829 / £73,145 = 59.9%, so £43,829 matches the 2h stack, but the sentence giving £43,829 itself names no duration.
